docs.title: User guide
docs.text: This guide shows you how to sign in, start a GPU workspace, manage projects and groups, use storage, and ask the admins for more.

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text:
• Start a GPU workspace (JupyterLab or VS Code) with storage that keeps your files
  • Open a GPU desktop or Isaac Sim in your browser
  • Manage projects: GPU/CPU/memory quotas, config files, members
  • Work in a group with shared storage
  • Send a request for more resources, storage, or an image
  • Read announcements about maintenance and rule changes
  • Check your quota and running GPU jobs on the Home dashboard

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A current browser (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari)
  • An account from a platform admin
  • VPN access (the platform is on a private network)
  • The acceptable use rules, read once

docs.title: First steps
docs.text:
Follow the Getting started guide. It takes you from VPN setup to your first workspace.

First-time checklist

  • [ ] Connect to the VPN
  • [ ] Sign in at https://dashboard.cscc.nthu.edu.tw
  • [ ] Look at the Home dashboard
  • [ ] Check your project's GPU quota under Projects
  • [ ] Launch a workspace

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Role What it can do User Use resources within the project's quota Manager Manage projects and groups, and open some admin pages Admin Everything

See Concepts and roles for the full permission tables.

docs.title: Announcements
docs.text:
Announcements are messages from the admins to everyone. They show up as banners on the dashboard and stay on the Announcements page until they expire. A scheduled announcement stays hidden until its publish time.

Who can use it: everyone who is signed in.

docs.title: Where announcements appear
docs.text:
Location What you see Home Dashboard Pinned or unread announcements at the top of the page. Sidebar → Announcements All current announcements, with All and Unread filters. Modal view The full title, text, priority, publish date, and expiry date. Overview popup Unread announcements pop up one at a time when you open or reload Overview. Pinned ones come first, then Critical, Warning and Info, newest first. Other pages do not pop up. Notification bell The bell in the header counts unread announcements and lists the latest three above your notifications.

Announcements have a priority: info, warning, or critical. Critical ones are usually about maintenance, a service problem, or something you must do.

docs.title: Read and acknowledge
docs.text:
1. Open Announcements from the sidebar, or click View all on a dashboard banner.
  2. Select an announcement to open the detail modal.
  3. Select I've read this. Only this marks it as read. Just opening it does not.

Closing one with ✕, Escape, or a click outside only hides it for now. It comes back next time you open Overview. Hiding a banner does not mark it as read either.

The button waits until your read is saved. If saving fails, keep the notice open and try again. Your read status follows you across tabs and devices. Reading the same notice twice counts once. Admins can see who has read a notice and when they first read it.

A new announcement updates the bell right away, and pops up if you are on Overview. If the live connection drops, the page checks about once a minute and when you come back to the window. Dates are in Taipei time.

A pinned announcement can keep showing after you read it, until an admin unpins it or it expires.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
Why did an announcement disappear?

It probably expired, or an admin removed it.

Can I reply to an announcement?

No. To ask about a notice or get help, send a request.

docs.title: Command Line Interface
docs.text:
Use cscc-cli to sign in, build images, follow build logs, run docker commands in the IDE and manage your API tokens from a terminal.

Who can use it: everyone who is signed in.

docs.title: Login
docs.text:
On a new machine, tell the CLI the API URL with --api-url or CSCC_API_URL. It's fine to include /api/v1. The CLI cleans it up.

cscc-cli login --api-url https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw --username alice

The CLI asks for your password. Unlike the dashboard, it needs no CAPTCHA.

After you sign in, the CLI saves a cscc_... API token in a config file on your machine that only you can read. The token itself shows only once, when it is created.

To name the token:

cscc-cli login --api-url https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw --username alice --name workstation

A token name can be up to 100 characters. Without --name, the name is cscc-cli.

docs.title: Import a dashboard-created token
docs.text:
You can also create a token in the dashboard under Settings → API Key & CLI and import it into cscc-cli:

cscc-cli login --api-url https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw --token cscc_...

The CLI checks the token before it saves it. Use this when you're already signed in to the dashboard and don't want to type your password in a terminal.

docs.title: Stateless token override
docs.text:
For scripts, set CSCC_API_TOKEN instead of saving a config file:

CSCC_API_URL=https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw CSCC_API_TOKEN=cscc_... cscc-cli whoami

CSCC_DEV_TOKEN still works but is deprecated. Use CSCC_API_TOKEN in new scripts.

docs.title: TLS / Internal CA
docs.text:
Official cscc-cli releases already trust the platform's certificate, so you usually don't need to set anything. If the platform certificate changes, download the latest CLI before you reconnect.

Use the variables below only for custom builds and TLS troubleshooting:

Env Description CSCC_API_URL API base URL, e.g. https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw/api/v1 CSCC_API_TOKEN Optional stateless cscc_... token override CSCC_API_CA_CERT_PATH One or multiple PEM files separated by , or ; CSCC_API_TLS_SERVER_NAME Optional TLS SNI name (fallback to config if not set) SSL_CERT_FILE Path to a PEM file containing the internal root CA REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE Alternative env path for a PEM bundle containing the internal root CA

Example:

CSCC_API_CA_CERT_PATH=/Users/me/platform-internal-root-ca.pem \
  cscc-cli login --api-url https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw --username alice

docs.title: Check Identity
docs.text:
cscc-cli whoami

This checks your saved token and prints your user and role. Role changes apply right away.

docs.title: Build Images
docs.text:
Upload mode is the default. Give it a folder, a .tar.gz or a .zip:

cscc-cli build --project <project-id> --name trainer --tag v1.0.1 .
cscc-cli build --project <project-id> --name trainer ./context.tar.gz

If you give it a folder, the CLI packs it into a .tar.gz for you. Either way, the Dockerfile must sit at the top level.

Dockerfile-only mode works like pasting a Dockerfile in the dashboard:

cscc-cli build --source dockerfile \
  --project <project-id> \
  --name trainer \
  --tag v1.0.1 \
  --dockerfile ./Dockerfile

cat Dockerfile | cscc-cli build --source dockerfile \
  --project <project-id> \
  --name trainer \
  --dockerfile -

Options:

Option Description --project Project ID the image build belongs to --name Short image name, for example trainer-api --tag Optional image tag. Omit it to use the platform default --source upload or dockerfile --dockerfile Dockerfile path, or - for stdin, when --source dockerfile --build-arg Dockerfile ARG override as KEY=VALUE; repeatable --follow=false Submit the build without streaming logs

docs.title: Build arguments
docs.text:
Pass Dockerfile ARG values at build time with --build-arg KEY=VALUE. Repeat the flag for more than one. It works with upload and dockerfile builds. A KEY starts with a letter or underscore and contains only letters, digits and underscores.

cscc-cli build --project <project-id> --name trainer --tag v1 \
  --build-arg HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx \
  --build-arg MAX_JOBS=4 \
  .

Use it to keep secrets and settings out of the Dockerfile you commit (for example ARG HF_TOKEN), or to limit compile parallelism (MAX_JOBS, FLASH_ATTN_MAX_JOBS, …) so a heavy build fits the shared build engine.

Anyone who can inspect the build can see build args. Don't put anything very sensitive in them, and replace any token you pass this way once the build is done.

docs.title: Shared build queue
docs.text:
Everyone shares one build engine, and it runs one build at a time. Each build gets a fixed amount of CPU, memory and scratch space. You can't change it.

The build engine shuts down when nobody has built for a while. The first build after that waits about a minute for it to start.

After you submit, --follow=true (the default) waits for the logs, shows them, and stops when the build reports completed, failed or deleted.

The CLI gets the API address from --api-url at login, then CSCC_API_URL, then its saved config:

export CSCC_API_URL=https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw

Builds and logs use the token from cscc-cli login. You need nothing else. The project must have Image Build Permission turned on, and your project role must allow builds.

docs.title: Using docker in the IDE
docs.text: Your Jupyter and VS Code workspaces have a docker command that works like Docker. Each container starts next to your workspace, in the same project, and counts toward the project's quota. Nothing runs inside the workspace itself.

docs.title: Sign in
docs.text:
A workspace started after the platform update needs no sign-in. docker uses the workspace's own identity.

A workspace started before the update keeps the old behavior: every container is a separate job, and you sign in with cscc-cli login. docker then prints restart your workspace for full docker support. Delete the workspace and start a new one. Files in your storage are kept.

docs.title: Run a container
docs.text:
docker run --rm alpine echo hello
docker run -d --name web -p 8080:8000 python:3.12 python -m http.server 8000
curl localhost:8080
docker ps
docker logs -f web
docker stop web

Output streams to your terminal, and the command exits with the container's exit code.

Without -t, Ctrl-C works like Docker's signal proxy. The first press sends SIGINT to the container's main process (the image needs /bin/sh; without one, the container is stopped instead). The second press stops the container (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10 seconds). The third press detaches and leaves it stopping in the background. With -t, Ctrl-C goes to the program in the container.

docker run -d waits until the container runs, showing Waiting: …, and then prints its ID. If the container can't start, it prints the reason, removes the container and exits 125. Press Ctrl-C to stop waiting: the container keeps starting.

docs.title: What works like Docker
docs.text:
• Only the paths you mount are visible inside the container. Mount a folder with -v SRC:DST[:ro] or --mount type=bind,source=SRC,target=DST. Write a relative SRC as ./data or ../data: a bare data means a named volume, which doesn't exist. -v creates SRC if it doesn't exist; --mount fails.
  • SRC must be under your home folder or a group storage folder. Read-only storage stays read-only inside the container. Named volumes don't exist.
  • The image's own WORKDIR, ENTRYPOINT and CMD apply. Your command after the image name replaces CMD, and --entrypoint replaces the entrypoint.
  • Without -u, a container runs as the numeric USER the image declares (for example USER 101). If the image declares no USER, or only a name such as USER app, it runs as user 1000, the same user as your workspace, so files it writes in your storage stay editable in the IDE. -u 0, and an image that declares USER 0, run as root only when the project allows root containers (and, for a group's project, the group does too). Otherwise the container runs as user 1000.
  • A container gets 1 CPU and 4 GiB of memory unless you set --cpus and -m. --shm-size sets the size of /dev/shm.
  • -e KEY=VALUE, -e KEY (copies your value), --env-file, -w, --rm and -d work as in Docker.
  • --name takes 2 to 63 letters, digits, _, . and -, and must start and end with a letter or digit.
  • --entrypoint "" clears the image's entrypoint. Then give the command after the image name.

docs.title: GPUs
docs.text:
Command What you get docker run --gpus all … or --gpus N The container shares your workspace's GPU and adds no GPU quota or GPU hours. N can't be more than the workspace has. --gpus device=0,1 picks cards by index, not by UUID. docker run --keep --gpus N … N new GPUs for the container, from your project's quota and plan, in the same queue as the workspace. They count toward GPU hours. With --keep, --gpus takes a number only.

A workspace without a GPU refuses --gpus all and --gpus N with this workspace has no GPU to share; use --keep --gpus N to allocate one for the container.

A container that shares the workspace's GPU uses the same card, so it shares the card's memory with the workspace.

docs.title: Containers and the workspace
docs.text:
A container lives and ends with its workspace. When the workspace stops, its containers stop too. That covers deleting the workspace, the idle limit, the runtime limit and a pause. A workspace that resumes after a pause doesn't bring them back.

A running container counts as activity. The workspace isn't stopped for being idle while one runs.

--keep detaches a container from the workspace. It keeps running after the workspace stops and counts as an ordinary job against your project's job limits. It can't share the workspace's GPU. Stop it with docker stop.

A container that ends stays in docker ps -a, with its logs, for 24 hours. Then it disappears. docker ps -a lists the containers you started in this project from all your workspaces, and the name of a listed container stays taken.

A container that stopped because its workspace stopped shows as Exited (137). Its logs are gone, and docker logs answers can not get logs from container which is dead or marked for removal.

--rm removes the container as soon as docker run has shown its exit code. For a container started with -d, the platform removes it about a minute after it exits. Without --rm, docker rm or docker container prune removes finished containers earlier.

docs.title: Stop, kill and remove
docs.text:
• docker stop sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10 seconds. -t is accepted, but the 10 seconds are fixed. The container stays in docker ps -a as Exited (143) or Exited (137), and its logs remain.
  • docker kill sends KILL through the same path as docker stop: SIGTERM first, then SIGKILL after 10 seconds. A program that handles SIGTERM exits with 143 or 0, so the exit code isn't always 137. The container stays in docker ps -a. docker kill -s HUP (or another signal such as USR1 or INT) goes to the container's main process through a shell, so the image needs /bin/sh. The program ignores the signal unless it handles it. If the signal can't be delivered, you get could not deliver SIGHUP: ….
  • docker rm removes a finished container. docker rm -f kills a running one first.

docs.title: Ports and the browser
docs.text:
-p 8080:8000 forwards port 8080 of the workspace to port 8000 of the container. In the workspace terminal:

curl localhost:8080

The port is open on localhost only, never to other machines, and only TCP works. -p 8000 alone picks a free port; docker port web shows which. If another program already uses the port, the run fails with port is already allocated before the container starts. Forwarding keeps working after you press Ctrl-C and ends when the container exits.

To open the app in your browser, start from the workspace address (click Open). It looks like this:

https://<platform host>/api/v1/ide/proxy/<workspace name>/

Add proxy/8080/ to it:

https://<platform host>/api/v1/ide/proxy/<workspace name>/proxy/8080/

This works the same in JupyterLab and VS Code workspaces. Keep the trailing slash. The platform removes proxy/8080 before the request reaches your app. An app that links to absolute paths such as /static/app.js can't load those files through this address. Use relative links, or set the app's base path to the full address.

docs.title: Interactive containers, exec and copy
docs.text:
docker run -it ubuntu bash
docker exec -it web sh
docker attach web
docker cp ./results.csv web:/tmp/
docker cp web:/var/log/app.log .
  • -it opens a terminal in the container. Press Ctrl-P, then Ctrl-Q, to leave a terminal session without stopping the container.
  • docker exec runs a command in a running container. It takes -i, -t, -d, -e and -w, but not -u. -e values travel in the command line, so they can appear in the platform's API logs. Pass secrets through a file in your storage instead.
  • docker attach joins the container's main process.
  • docker cp copies files in both directions through tar, so the container's image needs tar. Links are copied as links and are never followed: a copy refuses to write through one, and refuses a destination that is itself a link. It also refuses to replace a folder with a file, or a file with a folder, as Docker does.
  • An exec or attach session ends after 24 hours.

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
docker build -t myimg .
docker run myimg
docker images

docker build uploads the folder, builds it on the platform and stores the image in your project. It works in every project, and the FROM image can come from any registry. The platform scans base images for security problems automatically, so nothing needs approval first. -f takes a Dockerfile from any path, and --build-arg KEY=VALUE works as in Docker. After the build, a bare name such as myimg or myimg:v2 (no registry, no /) starts your build instead of a public image of the same name. docker images lists your project's builds. A .dockerignore in the folder works as in Docker, and the Dockerfile is always sent.

Building needs the Project Manager role or above, and image builds must be turned on for the project (Image Build Permission), like cscc-cli build.

The platform checks every image's security before the container starts. While it runs, docker run shows Waiting: image security check…. During weekday working hours the platform limits how fast it downloads from the internet, so the first start of a large image can take much longer then. docker pull only prints a reminder, because the platform fetches images when a container starts.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Limit Value Size 1 CPU and 4 GiB per container by default Project quota Container CPU, memory and GPU count toward your project's quota, and GPUs also toward GPU hours. A container that shares the workspace's GPU adds none. Containers per workspace 50 running or waiting. --keep containers have their own limit of 50 per project member. Beyond it, docker run fails with too many containers. Running at once Twice your project's per-user job limit for you in one project (20 when the project sets none), counting your workspace and its containers. Finished containers that aren't removed yet count toward a total of 60. Job limits A container that runs with its workspace doesn't count toward your project's concurrent job limit. A --keep container does. Finished containers Listed in docker ps -a, with their logs, for 24 hours after they finish. --rm, docker rm and docker container prune remove them sooner. Environment values -e values go straight to the container. Other project members can't see them.

Pausing

When the platform pauses a workspace to free its GPU (see Paused instead of stopped on the Concepts & Roles page), it stops the workspace's containers first, and the pause goes ahead. The containers don't come back when the workspace resumes.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command What it does docker run Starts a container. Takes -d -i -t -e --env-file -v --mount -w -u --cpus -m --gpus --name --rm --keep --entrypoint -p --shm-size. --pull and --platform are accepted and only print a note. docker exec, attach, cp Run a command in, join, or copy files to and from a running container docker ps [-a] [-q] [--format] [-f] List your containers in this project, from all your workspaces. -a adds the ones that finished in the last 24 hours. docker logs [-f] [--tail N] [-t] [--since] Show a container's output docker stop [-t N], kill [-s SIGNAL], rm [-f] Stop (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10 seconds), send a signal, or remove containers docker wait, inspect, port Print exit codes, details or published ports docker build, images, pull Build an image, list your project's builds, print a reminder docker container ls, rm, prune, docker system prune The long forms. prune removes finished containers only. docker info, version Show your project, queue and GPUs

These don't exist, and each prints a line saying what to do instead:

Not supported Why compose, network, volume There is no multi-container runtime, no user-defined network and no named volume. Start each service with docker run -d, and mount folders from your storage. push, commit, save, load, tag, rmi Images stay in your project. Use docker build -t NAME:TAG. start, restart, pause, unpause A finished container can't start again. Run a new one. stats, top, events The platform doesn't collect them. Use docker exec NAME top, or docker ps and docker wait. login The workspace is already signed in. -P, --network, --privileged, --cap-add, --device, --restart, --ipc, --pid, UDP ports, exec -u Containers share the platform's network, run isolated, never run privileged, and can't add Linux capabilities.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: What you see What it means Waiting: image security check… stays on screen The container hasn't started. A new image waits for its security check, and a busy queue waits for resources. Leave the command open, or run with -d and follow it with docker logs -f. Exit code 125 The container never started: the image couldn't be fetched (for example pull access denied), was rejected by the security check (the reason starts with Image security check failed), or an option was invalid. The reason prints above the exit, and the container is removed for you. Exit code 126 or 127 The command in the image isn't executable (126) or doesn't exist (127). Check the image's ENTRYPOINT and your command. Exit code 143 docker stop, docker kill or Ctrl-C ended the container with SIGTERM. Exit code 137 The container was killed. It ran out of memory (docker inspect NAME shows "OOMKilled": true, so raise -m), it ignored SIGTERM for 10 seconds, or its workspace stopped. Permission denied or Operation not permitted right after start, for an image such as nginx The image's main process needs root, and the image declares no numeric USER, so the container runs as user 1000. Add -u 0 in a project that allows root containers, or use an unprivileged variant of the image, for example nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged. port is already allocated A program or another container already uses that port of the workspace. Pick another host port, and check docker ps. Conflict. The container name "/web" is already in use A container with that name still exists, even if it finished in the last 24 hours. Run docker rm web, or choose another name. Invalid container name Use 2 to 63 letters, digits, _, . and -, starting and ending with a letter or digit. can not get logs from container which is dead or marked for removal The container's logs are gone: its workspace stopped, or it was removed. this workspace has no GPU to share The workspace has no GPU. Use --keep --gpus N, or start a workspace with a GPU. is outside your workspace storage or named volumes are not supported Mount a folder under your home or a group storage folder. invalid or expired workspace token Retry once. If it persists, delete the workspace and start a new one. restart your workspace for full docker support The workspace is older than the update. Delete it and start a new one.

docs.title: Token Management
docs.text:
List your active API tokens:

cscc-cli tokens list

Revoke a token by ID:

cscc-cli tokens revoke <token-id>

Sign out on this machine:

cscc-cli logout

Logging out revokes the token you're using and removes it from the config file. Certificate settings you added by hand stay, so you can sign in again without redoing them.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
Setting Default Notes Token lifetime 90 days Make a new token when the old one expires Active tokens per user 20 Revoke unused tokens if you hit the limit Failed sign-ins before lockout 5 Applies to both the dashboard and the CLI Lockout duration 15 min Wait, or ask an admin to unlock your account

Admins can change these values.

docs.title: Concepts & Roles
docs.text: How groups, projects, workspaces and storage fit together, and what each role can do.

docs.title: How things fit together
docs.text:
A group holds projects. A project runs workspaces and uses storage.

Item What it is Group A team or lab. It has shared storage and can be a member of projects. Project Where your resources live. It holds the GPU/CPU quotas, config files, and deployments. Workspace JupyterLab or VS Code in your browser. It uses the project's quota. Storage volume Disk space that keeps your files after a workspace restarts.

docs.title: Quota and resource plans
docs.text:
An admin gives each project a Resource Plan. When you start a workspace, the platform first checks the project quota and your own quota.

A plan also sets:

  • Allowed GPU models. The launch form only shows these.
  • A Schedule Window (when you can start work) and optional Burst Windows (when priority queues are open). See Plan Window below.
  • One or more queues you can pick, each with its own priority, preemption and GPU model rules.

docs.title: Scheduling queues, priority, and preemption
docs.text:
Every workload picks a scheduling queue. A queue has a priority, may be preemptible, and may have a deserved GPU number:

Concept Meaning Priority When GPUs are scarce, higher-priority queues go first. Preemptible Work in this queue can be stopped to free GPUs for higher-priority queues. Deserved GPU The number of GPUs the queue keeps even when other queues compete. 0 means none is guaranteed, so this queue is the first to give GPUs up.

The workspace and deploy forms list the queues your project plan allows. The default queue also needs an active plan that allows it.

docs.title: Paused instead of stopped
docs.text:
When a preemptible workload uses one GPU and runs as a single process, the platform pauses it instead of stopping it: its memory and GPU state are saved, the GPU is handed to the higher-priority job, and the workload continues from the same point once that GPU is free again, on the same node. The status shows Paused while it waits, and you get a bell notification when it pauses and again when it resumes. A pause can wait up to 7 days; after that the workload is stopped and reported as preempted.

Limits you should know:

  • Only single-GPU, single-process workloads are paused. Multi-GPU jobs, jobs that share GPU memory between processes, and jobs using CUDA unified memory are stopped as before.
  • Open network connections are closed at the pause. Reopen the notebook or SSH session after the resume; a training script that streams to an external service must reconnect on its own.
  • Work done in the last few minutes before the pause may be repeated after the resume. Writes to databases or object storage in that window can happen twice.
  • Untick Allow pausing when preempted in the deploy or workspace form for a workload that must never be paused; it is then stopped instead. The same effect comes from the label platform-go/checkpoint: "false" in a deploy YAML.
  • A paused job shows Paused in Deployments and Workspaces with the time it was paused; the row comes back to Running on its own. A paused workspace cannot be opened, or started again, until it resumes. Delete on a paused workspace ends it for good; you can then start a new one.

docs.title: Plan window
docs.text:
A plan has two weekly time settings, both in Taiwan time (UTC+8).

Schedule Window is when you can start work. Outside it you cannot submit anything new, even on a priority queue. The default queue follows the same rule. Work that is already running follows the plan's stop policy.

Burst Windows open extra priority queues, but only while the Schedule Window is also open. If Burst Windows is empty, there are no priority hours.

When a burst window closes:

  • Work that already finished is not affected.
  • About 5–6 minutes later, work still running on a priority queue is not restarted. It moves to the plan's normal queue for the same GPU model and gets that queue's priority. It can only be preempted if that queue is Preemptible. You get a bell notification.
  • If the plan has no normal queue for that GPU model, the work is stopped instead, and you get a separate notification.

The scheduling limits still apply.

Example: the schedule is 09:00–18:00 and the burst is 13:00–15:00. Ordinary queues work from 09:00 to 18:00, and priority queues from 13:00 to 15:00. The dashboard counts down each one separately.

Priority is not a reservation

A priority queue puts you at the front of the line. It does not stop long jobs that are already running, so on a full cluster you may still wait for a card.

docs.title: GPU claims
docs.text:
You get a GPU through a claim. A claim says:

  • GPU model: which GPU.
  • SM share: how much of that GPU's compute you get, as a percentage.
  • VRAM policy: elastic shares GPU memory with other workloads. hard cap sets a strict limit.

There are two kinds:

  • Inline claim: made for you when you start a workspace. It goes away with that workspace.
  • Project GPU claim: you create it on a project's GPU Claims tab and reuse it across deployments. It takes GPU quota the moment you create it, but it only counts GPU-hours while a workload is using it.

A project config file points to a project GPU claim through a claim slot (for example train-a). The slot name is just a label. In the deploy dialog you choose which of your claims fills it. All replicas of a Deployment share one claim and count once. If only some replicas need a GPU, split them into separate Deployments.

docs.title: GPU-hour budget
docs.text:
A resource plan can also limit the total GPU time a project uses, on top of the GPU/CPU/memory limits above. One GPU-hour is one GPU running for one hour. Part of a GPU counts as that part of an hour.

An admin sets how often the budget resets for each project: monthly by default, or weekly, or every set number of hours. Your project's Overview tab shows how much you have used and when it resets. When the budget runs out, new GPU jobs and workspaces are blocked until the reset. Jobs already running keep going.
