docs.title: Storage permissions
docs.text:
• Group storage permissions come from the group. Group members always get them, and a project cannot change that.
  • The project's Storage page shows those permissions but you cannot edit them there.
  • To change a group member's access, use the group page. For project members who are not in the group, use the project page. People outside the project cannot be given storage access from the project.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text: Term Definition Storage volume Disk space that keeps your files after a workspace restarts Scheduling Queue A named set of rules for priority, preemption, queue windows, and which GPU models it can use Plan Window Your weekly hours (UTC+8). Burst Windows add priority queues within those hours Preemption Stopping work in a preemptible queue so higher-priority work can run GPU Claim Your hold on a GPU. A project claim takes quota when you create it and counts GPU-hours only while a workload uses it GPU-hour One GPU running for one hour. A plan's GPU-hour budget is the most a project can use before the budget resets (monthly by default) Config File A deployment definition. Every save makes a new version, and old versions never change SM share The percentage of a GPU's compute you get Resource Plan A template that sets a project's GPU, CPU and memory limits, allowed GPU models, and schedule window Workspace JupyterLab or VS Code in your browser

docs.title: GPU desktops
docs.text:
A GPU desktop is a remote desktop that runs on a platform GPU and opens in your browser: a Linux desktop for GUI tools, or an Isaac Sim session streamed live. You see the screen and use your own keyboard and mouse. The GPU stays on the platform.

Who can use it: members of a project where an admin has turned on Remote Desktop Permission. If none of your projects has it, the page says Remote Desktop is not enabled for any of your projects. Ask an admin.

docs.title: Where to find it
docs.text:
• Sidebar → Workspace → GPU Desktops lists every desktop in your projects, in any state, not only the ones you can connect to.
  • You cannot create a desktop on this page. You start it from a project config file, like a deployment. See Start a desktop below.

docs.title: Start a desktop
docs.text:
You need the Manager role in the project, the same as for deploying a config file.

  1. Open Projects → [your project] → Config and click New File.
  2. In the Resource Wizard, add a Pod (or Deployment with one replica) with one container and its image, CPU, and memory.
  3. Turn on the Remote desktop switch under the container. The platform runs your workload as a separate desktop in your browser. Your image is not rebuilt.
  4. Fill in the desktop fields:
Field What to choose Desktop type Linux desktop (your image, shown inside a desktop) or Isaac Sim WebRTC (the platform's Isaac Sim image, streamed) GPU device class The GPU model GPU reservation 25% GPU, 50% GPU, 75% GPU, or 100% GPU. Below 100% you share the card with others. 100% is all yours Bitrate profile Economy (1600×900, 30 fps), Default (1920×1080, 30 fps), or High motion (1920×1080, 60 fps). Pick Economy when you are off campus
  1. Click Save, then Deploy the version as usual. Pick a queue; the plan window applies.
  2. Go to GPU Desktops. Your desktop shows up as a row. When it says Ready, click Connect.

Rules for a remote-desktop workload

  • Use one container, one replica, and no GPU request or GPU claim of your own. The desktop fields above cover the GPU.
  • Isaac Sim WebRTC needs the platform's Isaac Sim image and the VPN. GPU reservation works the same as for a Linux desktop. Mount one storage volume, read-write, at /workspace, and nothing else. Set CPU and memory yourself, within the project quota. One session used about 10 cores and 19 GB.
  • Only storage volumes (personal or group) can be mounted. Other volume types are rejected.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
Status What it means What you can do Pending Waiting for a GPU and encoder slot Wait Starting Getting ready Wait Ready Running, ready to connect Connect Degraded Running, with a warning in the row (for example software encoding: slower and heavier on CPU) Connect still works Failed Could not start Delete, then deploy again Stopping Shutting down Wait Expired Its time ran out Delete, then deploy again when you need it

Each row shows the desktop name, project, GPU model, encoder, image, and the expiry time, with a status badge. A row that is not Ready shows the reason when there is one (red for Failed, amber for the rest). If the image has no graphics libraries, the desktop cannot open and the row has no Connect button. Failed and Expired rows have a Delete button.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
• Linux desktop: Connect opens the desktop in a new browser window.
  • Isaac Sim WebRTC: Connect opens the viewer at GPU Desktops → [desktop]. Click the stream to control it with your keyboard and mouse. Leave control gives them back to the browser, and Full screen fills the screen. Quality switches between 1080p and 720p; pick 720p when the picture stutters on Wi-Fi or off campus. Changing it reconnects the stream. Stay on the VPN. If the viewer says VPN media authorization expired, reconnect the VPN and reload the page. If it says The video stream did not start or The stream stopped, click Retry; if that keeps failing, delete the desktop and create a new one.

While the viewer is open, it renews its connection every 2 minutes. Closing the tab does not stop the desktop.

docs.title: Lifetime
docs.text:
• A desktop lasts at most 8 hours, or less if the project's Max workspace continuous runtime (Settings tab) or the queue's runtime limit is shorter. The row shows the expiry time.
  • A desktop nobody watches for 30 minutes is reclaimed to free the GPU. An open viewer tab counts as watching.
  • When it ends, files in the mounted storage volume stay. Everything else in the desktop is gone. Deploy the config file again for a fresh desktop.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
The GPU Desktops page is empty.

No desktop is running in your projects. Deploy a config file with Remote desktop turned on (see Start a desktop). If the page says Remote Desktop is not enabled, ask an admin to turn it on for your project.

The status stays Pending.

It is waiting for a free GPU slice or video encoder, and starts when one frees up. A 100% reservation waits for a whole free card.

The row says Degraded. Is it broken?

No. It runs, with the warning shown in the row. Usually that means software encoding because the machine has no hardware encoder. Connect works, but expect more lag.

Where are my files?

Only the mounted storage volume stays after the desktop ends. For Isaac Sim that is /workspace. Save your files there.

Can I keep the desktop for more than 8 hours?

No. Deploy again after it ends. You get the same mounted volume, so your files are still there.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Connect, sign in, launch your first GPU workspace, and find your files.

Who can use it: anyone with a platform account from an admin. Read the acceptable use rules before you start.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Requirement Details Browser Chrome, Firefox, Edge, or Safari (latest version) Account Username and password from your platform admin VPN app An OpenVPN-compatible app (Step 1)

VPN is required

The platform is on a private network. Connect to the VPN first, or the dashboard address will not open.

docs.title: Step 1 — Install a VPN app
docs.text: OS Recommended app Install Windows OpenVPN Connect Download installer from the official site macOS Tunnelblick or OpenVPN Connect brew install --cask tunnelblick Linux OpenVPN CLI sudo apt install openvpn or sudo dnf install openvpn

docs.title: Step 2 — Connect to the VPN
docs.text:
1. Get the VPN profile (Platform-VPN.ovpn) from your administrator.
  2. Import it into your VPN app:
    • Windows / macOS GUI: drag the .ovpn file onto the client window, or use Import Profile.
    • Linux CLI: sudo openvpn --config Platform-VPN.ovpn
  3. When prompted, enter your platform username and password (the same credentials you use to sign in).
  4. Wait until the app shows a green light or Initialization Sequence Completed.

docs.title: Step 3 — Sign in to the platform
docs.text:
1. Open your browser and go to: 
    https://dashboard.cscc.nthu.edu.tw
  2. Fill in the three fields:
Field Description Username Your platform account username Password Your platform account password CAPTCHA Type the 4-digit number shown in the image
  1. Click SIGN IN.

Figure 1: Login page with username, password, and CAPTCHA fields.

CAPTCHA

Click the CAPTCHA image to refresh it if it is hard to read.

docs.title: Step 4 — Explore the Home Dashboard
docs.text:
After you sign in, you land on the Home Dashboard.

Widget What it shows Platform GPU Available Free vs. allocated GPU units across the platform GPU Cluster Status How much of each GPU is in use right now; machines appear under anonymous labels Project count (header line) How many projects you belong to, and how many of them have a plan Resource Usage History Live quota usage for each project that has a plan Recent Activity Your recent requests My GPU Jobs Your running GPU jobs with GPU share, memory, and running time

Figure 2: Home dashboard showing GPU availability, GPU cluster status, and My GPU Jobs.

docs.title: Step 5 — Check your project
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Projects in the left sidebar (Workspace section).
  2. You get a personal project with your account. Look for the project named after your username.
  3. Click the project card to see its quota (GPU, CPU, Memory limits) and members.

Figure 3: Projects page showing personal project card with quota summary.

No project visible?

Ask your admin to add you to a project or group, or to check that your account is fully set up.

docs.title: Step 6 — Launch your first workspace
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Workspaces in the left sidebar.
  2. Click New Workspace.
  3. Fill in the launch form:
Field What to choose Project Your project (personal or team) Environment JupyterLab or VS Code Image One of the platform's images: Base Notebook, PyTorch, TensorFlow, CUDA Dev, or a "(Root)" variant CPU Number of CPU cores, for example 2 Memory RAM in GB, for example 8 GPU Number of GPUs Compute quota (%) How much of each GPU you get: 25% is a quarter of a card, 100% is a whole card GPU memory quota (%) How much of the GPU's memory you get; leave Follow compute on and it matches the compute quota Storage Volumes Tick the volumes you want. Personal storage mounts at /home/<your username>, group volumes at /mnt/shared/<volume name>
  1. Click Start.
  2. Wait for the badge to change from Starting (yellow) to Running (green).
  3. Click Open. Your workspace opens in a new browser tab.

Figure 4: Workspace creation form with project, IDE type, and resource fields.

Workspace won't start?

  • Check that your project still has quota left.
  • Ask your admin if the project's plan window is open right now.
  • GPU images take longer the first time you start one.

docs.title: Step 7 — Manage your storage
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Storage in the left sidebar (Resources section). The My Storage tab opens.
  2. Click Start FileBrowser.
  3. Click Open FileBrowser. A FileBrowser window opens. There you can upload, download, rename, and organize files.
  4. Files here stay when a workspace stops. Click Stop FileBrowser when you are done.

Figure 5: FileBrowser interface showing personal storage contents.

docs.title: Step 8 — Join a group (optional)
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Groups in the left sidebar.
  2. Look through the groups, or ask your admin to add you.
  3. Group members share a group storage volume. It is good for datasets and shared models.
  4. Group managers can set each person's access to shared storage (Read / Write / None).

docs.title: Running your own container
docs.text: A workspace is for hands-on work. For a long training job or a service, deploy a container from the project's Config tab instead. You need the Manager role in the project, and you already have it in your personal project. See Projects → Config file versioning.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
VPN shows connected but the dashboard does not open

Import the profile again and reconnect. Some VPN apps also need DNS update scripts turned on. Still stuck? Check that your firewall allows UDP port 31194, then ask your admin.

Can I connect to the VPN from more than one device?

Yes. Your laptop and phone can be connected at the same time with the same account. Once a day the VPN app asks for your password again. Enter it and carry on.

Advanced: checking the VPN connection by hand

Open a terminal and run nslookup dashboard.cscc.nthu.edu.tw. If the name resolves and the dashboard opens, you are connected.

On Windows, if OpenVPN shows connected but 192.168.109.1 is unreachable, open PowerShell and run route print | findstr 192.168.109. The output should include a 192.168.109.0 route through the OpenVPN adapter. If it is missing, re-import the latest Platform-VPN.ovpn. The profile pushes the platform DNS server for cscc.nthu.edu.tw and turns on block-outside-dns, so Windows uses only that DNS server while connected. Resolve-DnsName dashboard.cscc.nthu.edu.tw confirms platform DNS; http://192.168.109.1:30080 is a low-level connectivity check.

CAPTCHA is wrong but I typed it correctly

The code is 4 digits. If you cannot read it, click the image to get a new one.

Login fails with 'Invalid credentials'

Use your username, not your email address. If your password changed recently, the old one no longer works.

Workspace stuck in 'Starting' state

Usually the image is downloading for the first time. Big GPU images can take several minutes. If it is still Starting after 10 minutes, ask your admin if your project's plan window is open right now.

Session expired and redirected to login

Your sign-in expires after a while. Sign in again. Your workspaces keep running.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
A group is a team or a course. Members share group storage, and you can add a whole group to several projects.

Who can use it: everyone can belong to a group. Only platform admins create groups. Need a new one? Send a Request.

docs.title: Group membership model
docs.text:
A group has three roles. Your role also sets your default permissions on projects the group owns.

Role Add / remove members Set storage permissions Access group storage Admin ✅ ✅ ✅ Manager ❌ ✅ ✅ User ❌ ❌ ✅

Teaching assistants usually need Admin

Manager is enough to set students' storage permissions, but adding and removing members needs Admin. If you run a course, ask a platform admin for Admin.

docs.title: Groups list page
docs.text:
Figure 1: The groups list, one card per group.

Each card shows the group's icon, name, description, ID and created date. Click a card to open the group. Platform admins also see Edit group and Delete group buttons on the card.

Platform admins set group policies (Storage Policy, Build Registry Lane, Root Containers, Allowed host paths) under Admin → Groups. They don't show on the card.

docs.title: View a group
docs.text:
Click a group card to open its page. It has two tabs:

  1. Members: everyone in the group and their roles
  2. Storage: the storage volumes the group owns and their permissions

docs.title: Requesting a new group
docs.text:
Only platform admins see the Create Group button. To get a new group:

  1. Go to Requests → New Request.
  2. Say what the group is for, who will be in it, and how much group storage you need.
  3. A platform admin reviews the request, creates the group and makes you its group admin.

docs.title: Join a group
docs.text:
Only group admins and platform admins can add members. To join a group:

  1. Submit a request via Requests and select the type Access Request.
  2. Say which group you need and why.
  3. A group admin or platform admin reviews it and adds you.

No public browsing

You can't browse or search for groups. Ask your team which one to join.

docs.title: Add members to a group
docs.text:
Requires Group Admin role.

  1. Open the group and click + Add Members (top right of the Members tab).
  2. Search by username or email.
  3. Pick users from the results.
  4. Click Add Members.

To add a whole class at once, use Paste users. Paste the list into the box (separate names with new lines, commas, semicolons or tabs) and click Resolve Users.

The results only list people who aren't members yet, so you won't see existing members or blank pages as you flip through.

Figure 2: The Add members dialog.

docs.title: Storage permission inheritance
docs.text:
You set group permissions on the group page. Projects show them read-only.

The permission levels are Read, Write and None. Each group storage volume also has an Access Policy, which is the default for members you haven't set individually.

Key rule: if you are in the group, your permissions on a storage volume attached to a project always come from the group. A project can't override them. Project-level grants only apply to project members who are not in the owning group. On the project's storage page, permissions that come from the group show as read-only, with a badge that links to the group's permissions page.

Permissions only count for current members. When you leave a group, you lose access right away. At the end of a term, just remove people from the group. You don't need to touch each project.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
I can see a group but can't add members.

You need the Group Admin role to add members. Ask your group admin or a platform admin to raise your role.

Why are my storage permissions greyed out on the project page?

You're in the group that owns this storage, so the group sets your permissions. Open the group's Storage tab to see them.

Can I belong to more than one group?

Yes, as many as you need. Each membership is separate.

How do I leave a group?

Ask a group admin or platform admin to remove you. You can't leave on your own. You lose access to the group's storage right away. Your personal storage isn't affected.

docs.title: Home dashboard
docs.text:
The Home dashboard shows free GPUs, your quota use, your running jobs, and your recent requests.

Who can use it: all signed-in users.

docs.title: Widget reference
docs.text: Widget What it shows Refresh GPU Availability Card Free and used GPU units across the platform, plus a preemptible-queue count On page load and every 10 seconds GPU Cluster Status Anonymous GPU machine cards showing how much of each GPU is in use On page load and every 10 seconds Project count (header line) Number of projects you belong to, and how many of them have a plan On page load and every 10 seconds Resource Usage History GPU/CPU/memory quota used vs. allocated for each project that has a plan, plus plan-window status On page load and every 10 seconds; countdown ticks every second Recent Activity Your 8 most recent requests On page load and every 10 seconds My GPU Jobs Your running GPU jobs with GPU share, memory, and running time On page load and every 15 seconds

docs.title: Reading GPU availability
docs.text:
The GPU Availability Card shows how many GPUs are free right now.

Figure 1: Home dashboard showing GPU availability, resource usage, and active jobs.

  1. Read the allocated / total fraction, for example 6 / 8 GPUs.
  2. Free GPUs = total − allocated. At 0 free, a new workspace waits in line.
  3. The card also shows a Preemptible queues count. When every GPU is busy, higher-priority work can still start by stopping a lower-priority workspace in a preemptible queue.
  4. Admins also see a View Reports button that opens the Audit page.

Effective GPU units

The card counts effective GPU units, not whole cards. One GPU at 50% SM share counts as 0.5 GPU, and only while a workload is using it.

docs.title: GPU cluster status
docs.text:
Below the availability card, the GPU Cluster Status grid shows each GPU machine under an anonymous label:

  • A display label such as GPU node 1 and the GPU model
  • Each physical GPU, with its index and model
  • How many shares of that machine's GPUs are taken, such as 3 / 8
  • A status bar and usage percentage for each GPU

Check the grid before you submit to see which models are idle, or whether a machine has room for a part-GPU claim. The dashboard never shows other users' names or workload names.

docs.title: Resource usage history
docs.text:
The chart shows your usage in every project that has a plan. Projects without a plan are not listed. If none of yours has a plan, the chart shows a notice.

  • Each bar is one project.
  • The fill shows how much quota you have used (GPU hours, CPU hours, or memory).
  • Each project row shows whether its resource plan is always active, closing, opening, or expired.
  • Plan-window countdowns update every second. You do not need to refresh.

docs.title: Recent activity
docs.text: The Recent Activity panel lists your 8 most recent requests, with their tag and submit time. Click View All to open the Requests page.

docs.title: My GPU jobs
docs.text:
The My GPU Jobs table lists the GPU jobs (workspaces and deployments) you have running right now. One row is one job; a job that spans several cards is one row.

Column Description Status Always Running; finished jobs are not listed Job The last 8 characters of the job ID Project Owning project GPU Effective GPU share held, and how many cards it touches Memory GPU memory held, in GiB Running How long the job has been running

You cannot change anything in this table. Open or delete a workspace on the Workspaces page; manage deployments from the project's Resources tab.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
Why does the availability card show 0 GPUs?

The card shows effective availability. If every matching GPU or SM share is taken, it shows 0. When a workspace stops, its GPU is free again within about a minute.

Recent Activity is empty. Is something wrong?

No. It only lists requests you sent. Send one on the Requests page and it shows up here.

My running workspace is not in the jobs table.

The table refreshes every 15 seconds. If it is still missing after the next refresh, reload the page (F5).

docs.title: Acceptable use
docs.text: Compute and storage on the platform are for teaching and research. These rules apply to everyone with an account. The platform logs activity and access. For what each role can do, see Concepts & Roles.

docs.title: Accounts and access
docs.text:
1. Your account is yours alone. Do not give your account, password, API token, VPN profile, or keys to anyone, including lab mates, project partners, and TAs.
  2. When someone else needs resources, ask an admin to create an account for them, or add them to your project or group. Never share a login.
  3. Use a password of at least 8 characters, and not one you use elsewhere. You cannot reset it yourself. Ask an admin, and the new password works for the VPN too.
  4. Treat an API token like a password. Keep tokens out of code, notebooks, images, and Git repositories. Revoke tokens you no longer use under Settings.
  5. Five failed sign-ins lock you out for 15 minutes. Do not script sign-in attempts.
  6. Use the platform through the VPN and cscc.nthu.edu.tw addresses. Do not bypass the VPN or connect straight to other internal addresses or IPs.
  7. Do not send requests as someone else, and do not change projects or groups you are not part of.
  8. If your password may have leaked, you see data that is not yours, or you get a sign-in notice you did not cause, change your password and tell an admin.
  9. When your course ends or you leave the lab or the university, ask an admin to disable your account.

docs.title: Compute resources
docs.text:
1. Resources are for teaching and research. Do not use them for mining, password cracking, proxies or tunnels, or commercial services.
  2. Delete a workspace when you are done. Do not leave a GPU idle to hold your spot. A workspace stops on its own after the idle limit shown under the list.
  3. A GPU desktop lasts at most 8 hours, and one nobody watches for 30 minutes is reclaimed. When it ends, only files in mounted storage stay.
  4. One GPU-hour is one GPU running for one hour, with part of a card counted in proportion. When the budget runs out, new GPU jobs and workspaces are blocked. Running work is not affected.
  5. A GPU claim takes quota as soon as you create it, even before a workload uses it. Delete claims you are not using.
  6. Ask only for the GPUs you need, in the number and model you need.
  7. On a preemptible queue, higher-priority work can stop your workspace. Save progress to mounted storage and make your training resumable.
  8. Do not get around quotas, runtime limits, or scheduling rules. That includes auto-restart scripts and fake activity that stops the idle timeout.
  9. For resources beyond your quota, file a resource request under Requests.

docs.title: Storage and data
docs.text:
1. Only mounted storage stays: personal storage at /home/<your username>, group storage at /mnt/shared/<volume name>. Files saved anywhere else are gone when the workspace stops or is deleted.
  2. Platform storage is not backed up. Keep your own copy of anything you cannot lose.
  3. Stay within your quota. When the usage bar turns amber (70%) or red (90%), clear caches, dataset copies, and old checkpoints before you ask for more.
  4. Do not store files unrelated to teaching or research, such as personal media, personal backups, pirated software, or datasets of unclear origin.
  5. Group storage is shared. Work in your own folders, and do not change or delete other people's files. When you leave the group, you lose access to that volume.
  6. Before you store personal data, an unpublished dataset, or anything you must keep confidential, check its licence and the rules, and get your advisor's OK. Keep such data out of group storage and images.
  7. For files over 500 MB, download them inside a workspace with wget, curl, or rclone. Do not upload them through the browser.
  8. Deleting a storage volume erases its contents for good. Copy your data out before you leave the platform.

docs.title: Images, licensing, and external services
docs.text:
1. Use images from trusted sources. The platform scans images for security problems automatically. An image with a fixable critical vulnerability can be refused, and its job then fails with the reason "Image security check failed".
  2. Follow the licence of every piece of software, model weight, and dataset you use. Do not install or share pirated or cracked software.
  3. Do not put accounts, passwords, tokens, keys, or unlicensed data in the images you build.
  4. An image a project builds is for that project.
  5. Do not run unapproved services for outside users, such as public websites, file sharing, and proxy nodes.
  6. Do not scan, probe, or attack any machine or service, on or off the platform, including other people's workspaces.
  7. Do not turn off or get around the platform's security controls or logs.
  8. When you publish results, credit the platform's compute the way your institution requires.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text: If these rules do not cover your case, send a problem report under Requests or ask a platform admin.

docs.title: Projects
docs.text:
A project is where your resources come from. Every workspace you start uses a project's quota, and every config file and deployment belongs to a project.

Who can use it: everyone who is signed in. You get a personal project automatically when you register.

docs.title: Project page layout
docs.text:
Figure 1: Projects list in list view, the default.

The Projects page has two views:

  • List view (default) — a compact table with sortable columns
  • Grid view — cards with the project name, description, member count and GPU usage bar

Switch views with the icons at the top right of the toolbar.

docs.title: Create a project
docs.text:
You need the manage-projects permission to create a project. Without it, the New Project button is hidden, and the create page sends you back to your project list. Ask an admin to create a project for you. You already got a personal project when you registered.

  1. Click Projects in the left sidebar.
  2. Click New Project (top right; you only see it with the manage-projects permission).
  3. Fill in the project form:
Field Description Name Short identifier (alphanumeric, hyphens allowed) Group Owning group (required) Description Optional. What the project is for
  1. Click Create. The project shows up in your list right away.

Quota is assigned by an admin

A new project starts with zero GPU quota. Ask your admin, or send a Request, to have a Resource Plan attached to your project.

docs.title: Project detail tabs
docs.text:
Click a project to open it. Everyone sees the Overview, Config, Plan, Builds, GPU Claims and Resources tabs. Members, Storage and Settings show up depending on your role.

Figure 2: The project page, with the Overview, Config, Plan, Builds, GPU Claims and Resources tabs, plus tabs that depend on your role.

Tab Contents Overview Description, quota usage chart, GPU-hour budget, current plan, member summary Config Config files with versions. They describe what you want to run Plan The project's resource plan, schedule window, allowed GPU models and quota limits Builds The project's image builds: pick an archive or a Dockerfile, see the shared queue and read live build logs GPU Claims GPU reservations you create ahead of time and attach to a deployment later Resources Live GPU, CPU and memory use for each member. Expand a row to see what they are running Members / Storage Extra tabs, shown when your role lets you manage members, quotas or storage Settings Limits for every workspace in the project. See Project settings below

Who sees what: the Storage and Settings tabs need Project Manager or above. Only Project Admins see the Members tab. (Platform admins must switch to Admin View in the avatar menu to count as a Project Admin.) An Admin can't demote themselves, so a project always keeps at least one Admin.

docs.title: Project settings
docs.text:
The Settings tab (Project Manager or above) has limits that apply to every workspace in the project:

Field What it does Max workspace continuous runtime In seconds. A workspace that has run longer than this is stopped automatically. 0 means no limit (the default).

Click Save Changes to apply it. The limit also applies to GPU desktops started from this project.

docs.title: Build project images
docs.text: Use the Builds tab when the project needs an image of its own. The base image in your Dockerfile FROM line can come from any registry. The platform scans base images for security problems automatically, so there is no approval step. Project Managers and Project Admins can start builds if image builds are turned on for the project. Project Members can see build status and logs. A member can't start a build, but can delete the image from a finished build they started.

docs.title: Source options
docs.text: Source When to Use It Upload archive Upload a .tar.gz or .zip. Put the Dockerfile at the top level of the archive. Dockerfile only Paste a Dockerfile. The platform sets up the rest of the build for you.

docs.title: Build settings
docs.text:
Field Notes Image Name Short name, for example trainer-api. The platform makes the full registry path. Tag Optional. Leave it empty for the platform default, or use a version like v1.0.1. Build source Upload archive or pasted Dockerfile.

Builds go into a shared queue and run one at a time. Each build gets a fixed amount of CPU, memory and scratch space. You can't change it in the form, and it doesn't use your project or personal quota.

The build engine shuts down when nobody has built for a while. The first build after that waits in the queue for about a minute while the engine starts, then runs as usual. The message says it is waiting for the build engine.

The platform checks uploaded archives for unsafe paths and size limits before the build starts.

The build history shows status, source type, destination image and live logs. Failed builds show a short summary in the table. Click the log button for the full output. If a build is retried, the log view keeps the previous attempt's failure reason above the current one.

Each build row has icon buttons: Cancel build while it runs (or Delete image artifact once it has produced an image), Clear saved logs and Delete history record. Builders and project managers can clear saved logs for finished or failed builds. Build history and images are not touched. The member who started a finished build, or a project manager, can delete its image artifact. Clear my completed build images deletes every finished image you built in this project, and keeps the build history and saved logs. A tag ID that appears more than once is deleted once.

Delete history record removes only the history and saved logs. It doesn't delete the image artifact. Harbor frees the registry space in its daily garbage collection. A recently uploaded image may need two garbage collection runs before it can be removed.

Build access is project-governed

If you don't see the start form, either the project doesn't have Image Build Permission turned on, or your project role can't start builds. You can still see build history and logs. Ask a project manager or platform admin to change the project setting or your role.

docs.title: GPU Claims
docs.text: The GPU Claims tab lists GPU reservations you can create for a project before you deploy anything. A claim holds GPU quota as soon as you create it, but only counts GPU-hours once a running workload uses it. When a config file has a GPU claim slot, you pick a claim for it in the deploy dialog.

docs.title: Create a claim
docs.text:
Fill in the Create GPU ResourceClaim form and click Create:

Field Notes Claim name The name you use when you attach this claim to a deployment. Letters, digits and hyphens only. GPU device class The GPU model to reserve. The form starts with a specific model. Pick Any only if the model doesn't matter. GPU count How many physical GPUs this claim reserves. A claim with several GPUs is still one reservation. SM share Compute share from 1% to 100%. The effective GPU count shows next to the form. VRAM mode Elastic shares GPU memory with other workloads. Hard cap keeps to the percentage you pick. VRAM share Only used with Hard cap. The memory is worked out from the smallest card of that model.

Every replica of a Deployment shares the same claim. A 2-GPU claim is one 2-GPU reservation however many replicas run. Quota and GPU-hours count once per claim, not once per replica.

A claim that isn't attached to anything uses 0 GPU-hours but still counts against the project and per-user GPU quota. The table columns are Name, Owner, GPU, SM, VRAM, Status and Allocation, plus a delete icon. Status is Reserved (created, nothing attached), Allocated (a GPU is assigned) or In use by . You can delete unused claims, but not one a running workload is using.

Claim ownership

Project Members can create their own claims. Project Managers can also see and delete other members' claims.

docs.title: Plan window countdown
docs.text:
The Plan tab shows two countdowns, one for scheduling and one for priority, in Taiwan time (UTC+8). Schedule Window always decides when work can start.

  • Window closes in HH:MM:SS is how much time you have left.
  • Window opens in HH:MM:SS is when you can start work again.
  • Always active means no weekly schedule limit.

The deploy dialog warns you before scheduling closes. After it closes, you can't start new deployments, and switching queues doesn't help. Workloads already running follow the plan's stop policy.

If the plan has Burst Windows, you see Priority ends in HH:MM:SS or Priority starts in HH:MM:SS, based on where they overlap the schedule hours. Priority queues show up next to the ordinary queues only during that overlap. When burst closes, existing work keeps running and scheduling stays open. A deployment that is still running inside the burst window, or already finished, is not affected. About 5–6 minutes after burst closes, a deployment still on a priority queue moves to the plan's normal queue for the same GPU model and takes that queue's priority. It can be preempted only if that queue is marked Preemptible. You get a bell notification when this happens. If the plan has no normal queue for that GPU model, the deployment is stopped instead, and you get a separate notification. If a window changes while the deploy dialog is open, the dialog refreshes the queue choices, keeps your selection if it's still available, and clears old validation results.

A queue can also have a runtime limit. If the queue you picked has one, your workload is stopped automatically after that many seconds, and the bell shows a Runtime limit reached notification. An admin sets the limit. You can't raise or turn it off in your config file.

If the plan has a GPU-hour budget, the Overview tab also shows a GPU-hours bar. It shows the GPU-hours used this period against the budget, the reset period (monthly, weekly, or every N hours, set by an admin) and when it next resets (UTC+8). When the budget runs out, you can't start new GPU jobs or workspaces until the reset. Jobs already running are not affected.

docs.title: Config file versioning
docs.text: Every save creates a new version. Old versions are never overwritten, so you can always look at an earlier one or deploy it again. Edit or upload a config file, save it, and a new version appears. You can deploy any version.

docs.title: Working with config files
docs.text:
1. Go to Projects → [your project] → Config tab.
  2. Click New File, then upload a YAML file or paste content in the editor.
  3. Each save creates a new version.
  4. Click the History icon next to a config to view all versions.
  5. To deploy a specific version, click Deploy on the version row.
  6. In the deploy dialog, pick the scheduling queue. If the YAML has GPU claim slots, pick one of your reserved GPU claims for each slot. This applies to this deploy only.

Running instances show up in the project's Resources tab. A separate Deployments page at /projects/<project id>/deployments lists deployments in Personal and Members tabs. It has no sidebar link, so open it by URL.

A finished Pod is removed at most three days after it ends, and its entry and logs on the Deployments page go with it. The logs can disappear sooner, for example when a node restarts. A Job keeps its finished pods until you delete the Job. Save results, and anything else you want to keep, to a mounted storage volume while the run is going.

docs.title: Containers you can shell into
docs.text:
To open a Terminal in a container, the container has to keep running. A shell with no arguments, such as command: ["/bin/sh"], exits right away. The container then restarts again and again, and every terminal attempt fails.

Give the container real work:

command: ["sleep", "infinity"]

or keep the shell alive by turning on stdin and tty under Interactive shell in the Resource Wizard (stdin: true and tty: true in raw YAML). The wizard warns you when a bare shell would exit right away.

Once the container is running, open the project's Resources tab and click Terminal on the Pod row. Deployment and Job rows have no terminal button. Expand them to find the running instance they created.

docs.title: Deploy rules
docs.text:
Quota is checked against everything you already have going, so a workload still waiting to start keeps its share until it finishes or is removed. Config files can deploy Pod, Deployment and Job. Other kinds are rejected.

Every container must set both a memory request and a memory limit of at least 128Mi. Deploy and dry-run validation reject missing values. Always write the unit: a bare memory: "1" means one byte and is rejected.

docs.title: Asking for a GPU
docs.text:
A config file can ask for a GPU in two ways.

  • Inline GPU request. In the Resource Wizard, pick a GPU model in the container's resource settings. The platform counts it toward your quota, checks the model against your plan's allowed models, and sets up the GPU when you deploy.
  • Reusable GPU claim. In the Resource Wizard, choose Pick at deploy and give the slot a name such as train-a. The slot name is only a label. In the deploy dialog, you pick which of your own claims from the GPU Claims tab goes with it.

To give a claim to only some replicas, split them into separate Deployments. A config that asks for no GPU needs no allowed-model list and never gets a GPU claim.

Advanced: writing the YAML yourself

Leave the fields the platform manages out of your YAML: don't set metadata.namespace, metadata.generateName, metadata.ownerReferences or metadata.finalizers. For storage, use {{userVolume}} to mount your personal volume. Naming a volume directly works only in a group's project, and only for volumes that group already has.

  • Each pod gets one memory-backed /dev/shm, shared by its regular containers (not init containers), of up to 8 GiB or the pod's memory limit if that is smaller. It is skipped when any container in the pod already mounts something under /dev/shm.
  • An inline GPU request goes straight into the container's resource requests, for example nvidia.com/rtx6000: "1".
  • A GPU claim slot is an annotation on the Pod, or on the Deployment's template: platform-go/dra-claim-name: '{{ gpuClaimName "train-a" }}'. {{gpuClaimName}} with no name still works as the default slot. Two workloads can share a slot deliberately, or use different slots to get different claims.

Config files and deployments require Project Manager role

Only project members with the Manager role or higher can create, edit, deploy, validate, inspect or delete config-file instances.

docs.title: Managing members
docs.text:
1. Open the project and go to the Members tab.
  2. Click + Add Members (you need the Project Admin role).
  3. Search by username or email.
  4. Pick a role for each user:
Role What they can do User Launch workspaces, view configs Manager Edit configs, manage deployments Admin Add/remove members, set member quotas
  1. Click Confirm to save.

Project Admins can tick several rows to remove members, change roles or set per-user quotas all at once. Managers and Admins see everyone's quota. A Project User sees only their own. A quota of 0 means no limit for that member, but the project plan's cap still applies.

Group-inherited members. Members who joined through the owning group can be part of a bulk quota change, but not a bulk remove or role change. Change their membership and role in the group instead.

Removing a direct member also removes their workspace area in the project, any project storage permission overrides and their per-user quota. To remove a member who came through the group, remove them from the group.

docs.title: Group inheritance and effective project role
docs.text:
When a group owns a project, the platform works out your project role like this:

  1. If you were added to the project directly, that role wins (admin / manager / user).
  2. Otherwise, on a personal project, the owner counts as admin.
  3. Otherwise, your group role in the owning group is your project role. So a Group Admin acts as a Project Admin on every project the group owns, even if nobody added them to the project.

That's why a Group Admin can set per-user quotas on their group's projects, and see the bulk-select controls in the Members tab, without being added as a member.

When someone leaves the lab: ask an admin to remove them from the group. They lose access to every project they joined through that group. You don't need to clean up project by project.

docs.title: Deleting a project
docs.text:
Only a platform admin can delete a project, from Admin → Projects. The project page has no delete button. Ask an admin, or send a Request, and delete the project's workspaces first. What happens:

  • The config version history and deployment records are gone for good.
  • Storage volumes are not deleted. They stay on the Storage page.

docs.title: Resources tab
docs.text:
The Resources tab shows live usage for each project member:

Column Meaning User Project member GPU Effective GPU units currently used CPU Requested or observed CPU cores Memory Memory in MiB Pod (the running instance) How many that member has running now

Project Admins, Project Managers and platform Admin/Manager roles see every member. Regular Project Users see only their own row. Expand a row to see what is running, or to terminate what you're allowed to manage. Terminating a workload here frees the quota it was using.

On Pod rows, hover, focus, or tap the status badge to see recent events. This helps when a workload looks like it's still starting but is really failing to pull its image.

docs.title: GPU quota overview
docs.text:
The Overview tab shows a quota bar for each resource type:

Resource What It Tracks GPU Effective GPU units consumed vs. plan limit CPU CPU cores consumed by running workspaces Memory RAM consumed by running workspaces

If the GPU bar is full (100%), a new workspace waits in the queue until resources free up.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
I don't see a New Project button.

Only users with the manage-projects permission see it. If you don't have it, ask an admin to create a project for you. Your personal project was created when you registered.

How do I view old config file versions?

On the Config tab, click the clock icon (History) next to a config file. You see every past version with its time.

My project quota is 0 GPUs. How do I get more?

Send a Resource Request through Requests. An admin reviews it and attaches a Resource Plan to your project.

What's the difference between a workspace's GPU and a GPU Claim?

A workspace holds its GPU only while the workspace exists. A GPU Claim is a separate reservation that stays across deployments. Use one when several jobs need the same fractional GPU and you don't want them rescheduled each time.

Why is the Deploy button disabled?

Either the project has no active plan, or its schedule window is closed. The default queue doesn't get around this. Check the Plan tab for the next opening time.

docs.title: Requests
docs.text:
Send a request when you need something from the admins: more GPU quota, new storage, access to a group, a new feature, or a bug report.

Who can use it: all signed-in users.

docs.title: Request types
docs.text: Type When to use it Resource More GPU/CPU quota, more storage, or new resources Access Join a group, use a shared storage volume, or get a higher role Feature Suggest a feature Bug Report a problem Question Ask the admins something Other Anything else

docs.title: Request states
docs.text: State What it means What you can do Pending Sent, waiting for an admin Add details in the message thread Processing An admin is working on it Answer their questions in the thread Completed Done, and the thread is closed Send a new request if you need more Rejected Declined Read the reason and send a new request. An admin can also reopen it

docs.title: Submit a request
docs.text:
1. Click Requests in the left sidebar.
  2. Click New Request (top right).

Figure 1: New request form with request tag, subject, and description.

  1. Fill in the form:
Field Description Project Optional. Link the request to one of your projects so the admins can see its GPU quota. The project's GPU bar shows next to the picker. Request Tag Pick one: Resource, Access, Feature, Bug, Question, Other. Subject One line, for example "4 GPU units for project LLM-Training". Description Rich text with formatting, code blocks, and images. Drag screenshots in. Images can be JPEG, PNG, GIF, or WebP, up to 10 MiB each.
  1. Click Submit Request. It starts as Pending. There are no drafts.

Say why, how much, how long

For a resource request, give the project, the number of GPUs, the time period, and your research goal. The admins decide based on these.

docs.title: My requests
docs.text:
Figure 2: Requests list with type tags, status badges, and creation dates.

The Requests page lists everything you have sent: request tag, status badge, subject, and date. Click a request to open its message thread.

docs.title: Message thread
docs.text:
1. Click the request card.
  2. Type in the box at the bottom.
  3. Click Post Reply. Admin replies appear in the same thread.

Figure 3: Request detail page with the message thread.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
How long does review take?

Most requests are handled within 1–2 business days. If nobody has replied after three days, ask again in the thread.

Can I edit or cancel a request?

No. Add or fix details in the thread. Once it is Completed, the thread closes, so send a new request.

My request was rejected. Can I resubmit?

Yes. Read the reason, adjust, and send a new one. Mention the earlier request number.

I got no notification when my request was resolved.

Turn on Push Notifications under Settings → Notifications.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
On the Settings page you edit your profile, change your password, manage CLI API tokens, set notifications and pick a language.

Who can use it: everyone who is signed in. Open Settings in the left sidebar (Infrastructure section).

docs.title: Tabs
docs.text:
Figure 1: Settings page with the Profile, Security, Notifications, and Preferences tabs.

Tab What you do there Profile Edit your full name; see your username and email Security Change your password; create and revoke API tokens; copy CLI setup commands Notifications Turn notifications on or off; link Discord for direct messages Preferences Choose the display language

docs.title: Profile
docs.text:
• Full Name — you can edit it; it shows wherever your name appears
  • Username — read-only; your sign-in name

  • Email — read-only if your account comes from the school's account directory

  • Open the Profile tab.

  • Edit Full Name.
  • Click Save Changes.

docs.title: Change password
docs.text:
1. Open the Security tab.
  2. Type your Current Password.
  3. Type a New Password (at least 8 characters).
  4. Type it again in Confirm Password.
  5. Click Change Password.

One password everywhere

Your new password works for every sign-in, including the VPN. If your account is managed by an external identity provider, change the password there instead.

docs.title: API tokens and CLI
docs.text:
The Security tab is also where you get a token for cscc-cli.

The token table lists your active tokens with their prefix, last-used time and expiry.

  • Create token — makes a new token. You can give it a name. The full token shows once, so copy it before you close the dialog. The dialog also gives you a cscc-cli login --api-url ... --token cscc_... command to paste.
  • Revoke — kills a token. Any CLI using it fails on its next call.

A token lasts 90 days by default. You can have at most 20 active tokens.

Shown once

The platform doesn't keep the token in readable form. If you lose it, revoke it and create a new one.

Official cscc-cli releases already trust the platform certificate, and the commands here already use the right API address.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
There are two checkboxes:

Checkbox What it does Push Notifications Notifications in the dashboard about your requests and projects. Click Save Changes to save. Email Notifications Shown, but not saved yet. Whether email is sent depends on the platform's mail setup.

docs.title: Discord direct messages
docs.text:
If the platform has the Discord bot turned on, this tab also has a Discord direct messages panel. Click Link Discord and approve on Discord. You come back to this page, and a welcome message is already in your Discord inbox. From then on the bot sends you a direct message for every bell notification, even when the dashboard is closed. For example:

  • your workload is about to be preempted, or was preempted
  • one of your jobs finishes or fails
  • a workload is stopped by a runtime limit
  • a burst-window workload moves to normal priority, or stops because none is available
  • new announcements

In the bot chat, /jobs shows 10 jobs per page. Use Previous and Next to page through your history. Enter keyword to search job IDs, statuses and queue names. The search ignores upper and lower case, and it stays on as you turn pages. The active filter shows jobs still running. The recent filter starts with your latest finished jobs, and you can page back to older ones. /clear deletes the bot's regular messages. Replies marked "Only you can see" stay until you dismiss them in Discord.

Linking also adds you to the platform's Discord server. The bot can only message people who share a server with it. If Discord blocks the first message, allow direct messages from server members in your Discord privacy settings, then link again. Unlink stops the messages. The bell in the dashboard keeps working either way.

docs.title: Preferences
docs.text: Under Language, pick English or Traditional Chinese and click Save. The page switches language right away.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
The password fields are greyed out.

An external identity provider manages your account. Change the password there.

I forgot my password.

The sign-in page can't reset it for you. Ask a platform admin to reset it. The new password works everywhere, including the VPN.

My email is wrong.

Your email comes from the account directory. Ask an admin to update it.

Can I delete my account?

Only an admin can. Send a request and say what you need.

I lost my API token. Can I recover it?

No. Revoke it under Security and create a new one.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
A storage volume is a folder that outlives your workspaces. Files you save inside a mounted volume are still there after the workspace stops or is deleted.

A workspace with no volume keeps nothing

Personal storage mounts at /home/<your username>; each group volume mounts at /mnt/shared/<volume name>. Files saved anywhere else are lost when the workspace stops, restarts or is deleted. The platform warns you before it starts a workspace with no volume.

Who can use it: an admin creates personal storage, so not every account has it. Look at the My Storage tab on the Storage page. If it's missing, ask an admin. Group admins manage who can use group volumes, and only current group members can have permissions on them.

docs.title: Storage types
docs.text: Personal storage Group storage Owner You A group Created by Admin Admin, on request Who can use it You only Group members, by permission Best for Your datasets, notebooks, experiments Shared datasets, team work Managed from My Storage tab Group Storage tab

docs.title: Storage page
docs.text:
Figure 1: The Storage page with the My Storage and Group Storage tabs.

  • My Storage — your own volume, shown as a card with the file browser status (Stopped, Starting, Running, Stopping, Error), a usage bar and the file browser buttons.
  • Group Storage — volumes of the groups you belong to, in a table with these columns: name, status (Active means ready to mount, Terminating means it is being removed, Missing means the platform can't find it), file browser status, capacity (for example 50Gi), usage, access mode, your permission, group, created date and action icons.

A group volume stays mounted for the project even when you stop a workspace. It is released only when an admin removes it from the project or deletes it.

If the file browser status shows Error, the file browser stopped unexpectedly. Click Start FileBrowser (for a group volume, the icon in the Actions column) to restart it. Your files are not affected.

docs.title: Usage bar
docs.text:
The bar reads used / total Gi with a percentage. It turns amber at 70% and red at 90%.

Capacity is the space you were given. Usage is how much you have written. A dash (—) means the platform hasn't measured that volume yet. It doesn't mean the volume is empty. The numbers refresh every few minutes, so a big copy shows up a little late.

docs.title: Volume lifecycle
docs.text:
1. You ask for storage on the Requests page.
  2. An admin approves and creates the volume.
  3. The volume is attached to a project and appears in the workspace form.
  4. Your workspaces, jobs and deployments mount it. Your data is still there after a restart.
  5. An admin deletes it. The volume and its data are gone.

Deletion is permanent

Deleting a volume erases everything in it. Back up what matters before you ask for removal.

docs.title: Browse files
docs.text:
1. On the My Storage tab, click Start FileBrowser and wait until the badge shows Running.
  2. Click Open FileBrowser. It opens in a new tab.
  3. When you're done, click Stop FileBrowser.

For a group volume, use the icons in the Actions column: Start FileBrowser, then Browse, then Stop FileBrowser. If your permission on that volume is None, you won't see these icons.

Figure 2: The file browser, with upload, download and delete.

In the file browser you can open folders, upload (drag and drop, or pick files), download files and folders, create folders and delete. Deleting is immediate.

Large uploads

For files over 500 MB, don't upload through the browser. It has size and timeout limits. Download them inside a workspace with wget, curl or rclone.

docs.title: Mount storage in a workspace
docs.text:
1. In the New Workspace form, find the Storage Volumes section. It lists your personal storage and the group volumes attached to the project you picked.
  2. Tick the volumes you want.
  3. Click Start.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Each group volume has a permission for each user:

Permission What you can do Read Mount and read Write Mount, read, and write None Nothing. You can't mount or browse it

If a group admin sets None, it beats anything the project or group would otherwise give you. Clear it and your normal permission comes back. Ask your group admin to change permissions. Group admins can edit them in bulk on the group's Storage tab (see Groups).

Every group member sees the Permissions icon on a group volume, but only group managers and admins can open the permissions page. Everyone else goes back to the Storage page.

Your permission applies to everything you run, not just workspaces. If you have no permission on a volume, a job or deployment can't mount it either, even if you write its name in your own YAML. A volume that isn't attached to the project can't be mounted from that project at all.

Read-only means read-only. If your permission on a volume is Read, it is mounted read-only in every workspace, job and deployment. Writing readOnly: false in your own YAML changes nothing, because the platform sets it back. Being a project or group manager doesn't change it either. The manager role only skips the separate rule that keeps group volumes read-only for ordinary members.

docs.title: Ask for more storage
docs.text:
Only platform admins can create group volumes. Group admins can't. To get one, or more space:

  1. Go to Requests → + New Request.
  2. Pick type Resource.
  3. Say what you need: size, purpose and group name.
  4. Click Submit. An admin reviews it and creates the volume.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
My volume shows Pending. When can I use it?

It's still being created, which usually takes under a minute. After 5 minutes, contact an admin.

My volume is full but I see no large files.

In a workspace terminal, run du -sh /home/<your username>/*. The usual culprits are hidden folders such as .cache and .local, and notebook checkpoints.

The usage bar shows a dash.

The platform hasn't measured it yet. Check again in a few minutes. If it's still blank after an hour, contact an admin.

I deleted files but the usage bar has not moved.

The numbers refresh every few minutes. Wait a bit, then reload the page.

I see a group volume but cannot browse it.

You need at least Read on it. Ask your group admin.

Is my data still there after I delete a workspace?

Yes. Your data is only lost if the volume itself is deleted.

Can several workspaces mount the same volume?

Yes. Several workspaces can mount the same personal or group volume at the same time.

Files I uploaded in the browser do not show in my workspace.

Look under /home/<your username> (personal) or /mnt/shared/<volume name> (group). A volume is mounted when the workspace starts, but files you upload later show up right away. You don't need to restart.

docs.title: Workspaces
docs.text:
A workspace is a JupyterLab or VS Code environment with GPU access. It starts from one of the platform's images.

Who can use it: project members whose project has enough quota.

docs.title: Workspace states
docs.text:
State What it means What you can do Starting The workspace is downloading its image and starting. Wait 30–120 seconds Running The workspace is ready to use. Open or Delete Stopped The workspace isn't running (for example, it hit the idle limit or the runtime limit). Files in mounted storage are kept. Delete, then create a new one Error The workspace failed to start. Delete, then create a new one

There's no start or stop button. A workspace runs until you delete it or the platform removes it.

docs.title: Workspace list page
docs.text:
Figure 1: The workspace list with status badges.

Each row shows:

  • Workspaces — the workspace name, with the environment and project below it
  • Status — Running (green), Starting (yellow), Stopped (grey), Error
  • Image — the image it runs
  • Resources — the GPU count, or CPU for a CPU-only workspace
  • The last activity time
  • Open (only while Running) and Delete

Below the table, a notice shows the idle limit: Auto-stop after N minutes of inactivity. See Idle shutdown below for what counts as activity.

docs.title: Launch a workspace
docs.text:
1. Click Workspaces in the left sidebar.
  2. Click New Workspace (top-right).

Figure 2: The new workspace form, with project, environment, image, GPU and storage fields.

  1. Fill in the form:
Field Description Project The project this workspace belongs to. It decides which quota you use. Projects without a plan are marked (No Plan) and can't start a workspace. Internet Access Read-only. A banner under the project says whether workspaces in this project can reach the Internet (Enabled / Disabled). When it's disabled, the workspace can still reach platform services but can't download from outside. Environment JupyterLab or VS Code Image One of the platform's images for that environment: Base Notebook, PyTorch, TensorFlow, CUDA Dev, and their "(Root)" versions. Images you request or build for a project are for deployments, not workspaces. Root shell Makes you root inside your own container. You only see it when the project allows root containers (and, for a group's project, the group does too). Scheduling queue Pick one of the queues the project plan allows. See Scheduling queue and priority below. GPU How many GPUs. Pick No for a CPU-only workspace. GPU Model One of the models your plan allows. Other models are hidden. Compute quota (%) How much of each GPU's compute you get. 100% is a full GPU. Smaller values count as part of a GPU. If you pick a fractional GPU, it's filled in for you. GPU memory quota (%) How much of each GPU's memory you get. Leave Follow compute on to match the compute quota, or turn it off and set your own value. All workloads on one card add up to at most 100%. CPU / Memory Optional. Defaults to the plan's limits Shared memory (/dev/shm) Not a form field. Every workspace gets a /dev/shm of up to 8 GiB, or the memory limit if that is smaller. It lives in memory, so what you put there counts toward the memory limit. That's enough for PyTorch data loaders, NCCL and vLLM. Storage Volumes Tick the volumes to mount. Personal storage is at /home/<your username>; each group volume at /mnt/shared/<volume name>.

The platform picks the name. There's no name field.

  1. Click Start.
  2. The workspace shows as Starting. Wait 30–120 seconds while it downloads its image and starts.
  3. When the status changes to Running, click Open. The IDE opens in a new browser tab.

No storage selected

If you have no personal storage and tick no group volume, the platform shows This workspace will not keep your files before it starts. Everything you write is lost when the workspace stops, restarts or is deleted. Click Cancel and tick a volume, or click I understand, start anyway.

Idle shutdown

A workspace with no activity for the idle limit shown under the list is stopped automatically, so the GPU goes back to other people. It applies to every workspace, with or without a GPU. Only real activity in the IDE counts: opening pages, typing in the terminal, running a notebook. An open tab doesn't. A workspace that is still computing keeps running, even if nobody is at the keyboard, but one that is just idling (a background process using a fraction of a core) isn't computing. Delete the stopped one and create a new one. Files in mounted storage are kept.

Root shell

Root shell only makes you root inside your own container. It gives you no access to the platform or to other people's data. If you don't see the toggle, ask an admin to allow root containers on the project (and on the group, for a group's project).

docs.title: Scheduling queue and priority
docs.text:
Each workspace uses one scheduling queue. A queue has a priority, and it may be preemptible or have a deserved GPU limit. Admins set these.

Concept Effect on your workspace Higher priority When GPUs are scarce, it's scheduled before workspaces in lower-priority queues. Preemptible queue The platform can stop your workspace to make room for a higher-priority workload. Default queue The lowest-priority queue, used as a fallback. It still needs an active project plan, and the plan must allow it.

The launch form lists the queues the project's active plan allows. If the project has no plan, you can't start a workspace until an admin adds one. GPU workspaces are also checked against the GPU models your plan and queue allow, even if you leave the model blank and let the platform pick.

docs.title: Plan window
docs.text:
A plan has two separate weekly time settings, both in Taiwan time (UTC+8).

Schedule Window is when you can start work. Outside it, you can't submit new work, including on priority queues. Work that is already running follows the plan's stop policy. The default queue doesn't get around this rule.

Burst Windows give you extra priority queues, but only while the schedule window is also open. If Burst Windows is empty, there are no priority hours. A workspace that is still running inside a burst window is not affected, and neither is one that already finished. About 5–6 minutes after a burst window closes, a workspace still on a priority queue is not restarted. It moves to the plan's normal queue for the same GPU model and takes that queue's priority. It can be preempted only if that queue is marked Preemptible. You get a bell notification when this happens. If the plan has no normal queue for that GPU model, the workspace is stopped instead, and you get a separate notification. The scheduling limits still apply.

For example, say the schedule is 09:00–18:00 and the burst is 13:00–15:00. You can use ordinary queues from 09:00 to 18:00 and priority queues from 13:00 to 15:00. The dashboard shows the two countdowns separately.

Outside the schedule, Start is rejected. Wait for the next window, or ask an admin to update the plan. The project's Plan tab also shows both countdowns.

docs.title: Connect to your workspace
docs.text:
When the workspace is Running, click Open. Your browser connects straight to it. You don't need any setup.

  • JupyterLab opens at /lab. It's the standard Jupyter interface.
  • VS Code (code-server) opens at /. It's full VS Code in the browser.

Both IDEs come with tmux in the terminal. A tmux session keeps running when you close the browser tab, but it ends when the workspace is deleted or restarted.

Where to save your work

Code and notebooks saved under /home/<your username> (personal storage) or /mnt/shared/<volume name> (group volume) are still there after the workspace is gone. Files saved anywhere else are lost when the workspace is deleted.

Use $XDG_CONFIG_HOME, not a hardcoded ~/.config

Workspaces come with XDG_CONFIG_HOME=~/.local/config. Tools that follow it (code-server, pip config, gh, …) save their settings there, and the settings stay when you switch workspaces.

If you set up a tool by hand, use $XDG_CONFIG_HOME instead of a hardcoded ~/.config.

docs.title: Stopping a workspace
docs.text: You can't stop a workspace. To free the GPU, click Delete. The workspace is removed, and files in mounted storage volumes are kept. Create a new workspace when you need one again.

docs.title: Bulk delete (admins)
docs.text: Admins who manage workspaces can tick several workspaces and delete them together with the toolbar that appears.

docs.title: How GPUs are allocated
docs.text:
When you pick a GPU model and compute quota, the platform reserves that share of a GPU for your workspace.

  • GPU is how many physical GPUs you ask for.
  • Compute quota (%) sets the share that counts toward your quota and GPU sharing. The form shows Effective GPU, so you can see what counts against your quota.
  • GPU memory quota (%) follows the compute quota unless you set it yourself.
  • Quota counts every workspace you asked for, including ones still waiting to start.
  • Run nvidia-smi in your workspace to see which GPUs you can use.
  • To get a whole GPU or a specific model, pick 100% and a model your plan allows, or ask an admin to change the plan.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
The Open button doesn't appear even though status is Running.

The connection can take a few more seconds to be ready. Wait 10 seconds and refresh the page. If the button still doesn't show, the workspace is probably restarting again and again. Ask your admin.

My workspace stopped automatically.

The platform stops a workspace when it has no activity for the idle limit (see Idle shutdown above) or when it passes the project's runtime limit. Delete it and create a new one. Files in mounted storage are kept.

I see an error status. What do I do?

Delete the workspace and create it again. Usual causes: the image couldn't be downloaded, you don't have enough quota, or the GPU model you asked for isn't available. If it keeps happening, send a Request.

Can I have multiple workspaces running at once?

Yes, as long as their total GPU use stays within your project's quota.

My workspace was evicted with reason 'Plan window expired'.

The schedule window closed. Create a new workspace in the next window. Burst doesn't get around the schedule. But when only the burst window closes, the workspace isn't evicted. It keeps running, moved to the plan's normal queue for its GPU model.

Why are some GPU models greyed out in the launch form?

Your project's plan lists which GPU models are allowed, and other models are hidden. Ask a project manager to attach a plan that includes the model you need.
